title: Why the Semiconductor Industry Needs A Common Language For Functional Safety
gist: Accellera's Functional Safety Working Group has released the Functional Safety Language (FSL) 1.0 Draft Standard, a common machine-readable data model meant to replace spreadsheet- and document-based functional safety analyses (FMEDA, FMEA, FTA, DFA) in chip design, with public comments open through August 14, 2026.

insights.claim: Functional safety has shifted from a specialized engineering discipline into a fundamental design requirement as semiconductor devices become central to automotive, industrial, aerospace, and medical applications, meaning safety-data management now rivals safety-mechanism design in importance.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: Chip design tool and IP vendors serving safety-critical end markets should expect functional-safety data infrastructure, not just safety mechanisms, to become a competitive requirement.
insights.quote: The challenge is no longer simply implementing safety mechanisms—it is managing the safety-related information that must be created, shared, reviewed, and maintained throughout the development lifecycle.
insights.locator: As semiconductor devices become increasingly central

insights.claim: Functional safety analyses such as FMEDA, FMEA, FTA, and DFA are today largely stored in spreadsheets, proprietary databases, custom scripts, and tool-specific formats, and are often recreated or manually translated as they move between organizations, teams, and EDA tools.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: Manual translation of safety data across the supply chain is a hidden cost center and error source for chipmakers and their suppliers/customers — a candidate for automation tooling.
insights.quote: much of that information exists in spreadsheets, proprietary databases, custom scripts, and tool-specific formats
insights.locator: Today, much of that information exists

insights.claim: The lack of a common format for exchanging functional safety data causes duplicated engineering effort, limited interoperability between organizations and tools, reduced traceability and confidence, and increased risk of inconsistencies as designs grow more complex and supply chains more distributed.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: As chip supply chains fragment further (multi-vendor IP, distributed fabs/packaging), the cost of non-standardized safety data exchange compounds, favoring vendors who solve interoperability early.

themes.theme: Standards gap: compliance vs. data exchange

insights.claim: Established functional safety standards ISO 26262 (automotive) and IEC 61508 (general electronics) define what is required to achieve functional safety compliance, but intentionally do not specify how safety data itself should be represented and exchanged across organizations and tools — a gap the author argues has become increasingly apparent.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: Compliance with ISO 26262/IEC 61508 does not by itself guarantee interoperable safety data — this unaddressed layer is where new standards and tooling opportunities exist.
insights.quote: What these standards intentionally do not define is how safety data should be represented and exchanged across the many organizations and tools involved in product development.
insights.locator: The industry has long benefited from standards

insights.claim: Unlike design, verification, and manufacturing data, which are managed through automated tool chains, functional safety information management remains primarily a document-centric process, forcing engineers to spend time translating and interpreting data instead of doing safety analysis.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: Automating functional-safety data flows (vs. design/verification data, already automated) is a lagging but addressable efficiency opportunity inside EDA workflows.
insights.quote: Engineers frequently spend valuable time translating and interpreting data rather than focusing on high-value safety analysis.

insights.claim: The Accellera Functional Safety Working Group developed the Functional Safety Language (FSL) Standard as a common, implementation-level language and data model for creating and representing functional safety data, aiming to give safety information the same tool-chain consistency as design and verification data.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: A new Accellera standard creates a reference point EDA vendors, IP suppliers, and safety-critical chipmakers will likely need to support for interoperability going forward.
insights.quote: The industry needs a common, implementation-level language for functional safety data—one that enables safety information to move through the development ecosystem with the same level of consistency as design and verification data.

insights.claim: FSL initially focuses on FMEDA (Failure Modes, Effects, and Diagnostic Analysis) content, with a long-term roadmap to expand to related analyses such as FTA (Fault Tree Analysis) and DFA (Diagnostic Failure Analysis), and is designed to complement rather than replace existing safety standards like ISO 26262 and IEC 61508.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: Watch FSL's scope expansion beyond FMEDA into FTA/DFA as a signal of how broadly the standard will be adopted across the safety analysis stack.
insights.locator: FSL is designed to provide a standardized language

insights.claim: With a common representation of safety data under FSL, organizations could exchange information between EDA tools, suppliers, IP providers, semiconductor companies, and system integrators without relying on proprietary formats or extensive manual conversion.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: If adopted, FSL could reduce switching costs and integration friction between safety-critical chip suppliers and their customers, potentially benefiting smaller IP vendors currently locked out by proprietary interface requirements.
insights.locator: With a common representation of safety information

insights.claim: FSL is positioned to benefit four distinct groups: safety engineers get structured, consistent FMEDA creation with better traceability; design/verification teams get tighter integration between safety analyses and implementation; tool vendors reduce the need to build and maintain numerous proprietary interfaces; and the broader supply chain gets a consistent mechanism for exchanging safety data with fewer translation errors.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: EDA vendors currently maintaining many bespoke proprietary safety-data interfaces stand to cut integration costs if FSL gains adoption — a potential margin/efficiency tailwind for tool vendors like Synopsys, Cadence, and peers.

insights.claim: The author argues that standardized, machine-readable functional safety data (via FSL) becomes increasingly important as engineering organizations integrate AI-assisted workflows and more sophisticated verification methodologies, positioning FSL as infrastructure for future automation rather than just a file-format swap.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: As AI-assisted chip design tools proliferate, standardized safety data formats like FSL could become a prerequisite for applying AI/automation to safety-critical verification workflows — a theme to watch in EDA AI tooling roadmaps.
insights.quote: The goal is not simply to replace spreadsheets with another file format. It is to establish a foundation upon which future functional safety workflows can continue to evolve.

insights.claim: The Functional Safety Language (FSL) 1.0 Draft Standard from Accellera is open for public review, with the working group inviting industry comments through the Functional Safety Community Forum until August 14, 2026, before resuming formal activity in September 2026 to add a formal exchange format and expand FSL's scope.
insights.speaker: Alessandra Nardi
insights.so_what: Chipmakers, IP vendors, and EDA companies with a stake in functional safety tooling have a concrete, near-term window (through August 14, 2026) to influence the FSL 1.0 spec before it solidifies.
